There is a document in every church that reveals more about its true beliefs than any statement of faith, any mission statement, any carefully worded vision on the website. It is the budget. A church budget is a theological document, arguably the most honest theological document a congregation produces, because it records not what the church says it values but what it actually values, measured in the one currency that cannot lie: money spent. And most churches have never read their budget this way. They treat it as a mundane administrative necessity, a spreadsheet for the finance committee, when in fact it is a confession of faith written in dollars.

I want to argue that the way a church allocates its money is a direct expression of its theology, that the budget preaches a sermon every week whether anyone reads it or not, and that examining the budget honestly is one of the most spiritually revealing things a congregation can do. Because a budget cannot be spun. You can say anything you want in a sermon. The budget shows what you did.

## What a Budget Confesses

Consider what a budget actually records. It records priorities in their most concrete form. A church may say it prioritizes reaching the lost, caring for the poor, and discipling its people. But when you look at where the money goes, how much to the building, how much to staff salaries, how much to the poor, how much to missions, how much to programs that serve the existing members versus outreach that serves those outside, a different and truer picture often emerges. The stated priorities and the funded priorities frequently diverge, and where they diverge, the funded priorities are the real ones. Money is a lie detector. It shows what a church is actually organized to do.

Jesus said it directly, and it applies to institutions as much as individuals: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. This is not merely a diagnostic, it is not only that the budget reveals the heart. It is also formative: the budget shapes the heart. A church that spends nearly everything on itself becomes a self-focused church, regardless of its outward-facing rhetoric. A church that gives generously to the poor and to mission becomes a generous church, and its people are formed by the pattern of its spending into generous people. The budget is both a mirror and a mold. It reflects what the church is and shapes what the church becomes.

> You can preach any sermon you like. The budget preaches the sermon you actually believe. And the congregation is being discipled by the spreadsheet whether they ever see it or not.

## The Building Problem

The single largest line in most church budgets, after staff, is the building, the mortgage, the maintenance, the utilities, the endless costs of keeping a physical facility running. And this deserves honest theological scrutiny, because the amount of kingdom resource poured into physical structures is enormous, and its justification is rarely examined. There is nothing inherently wrong with a building; the church needs space to gather. But when a congregation of modest size is spending the majority of its resources maintaining a facility used a few hours a week, while giving a fraction to the poor and to mission, the budget is confessing a theology that few would defend out loud.

The early church had no buildings. It met in homes, and it poured its resources into people, into the poor, into the spread of the gospel, into the care of widows and orphans and the sharing of possessions so that none among them was in need. Somewhere in the long history of Christianity, the resources shifted decisively from people to structures, and the shift was so gradual that we have never noticed it as a theological choice. But it was one. Every church that spends more on its building than on the poor has made a theological statement about the relative value of edifices and image-bearers, and it is not a statement the New Testament would endorse. I say this as a pastor whose own church carries the weight of a building, and the conviction is uncomfortable precisely because it lands close to home.

## The Staff Question

After the building comes the staff, and this too is a theological matter deserving honesty. Pastoral and ministry staff are worthy of their wages; the laborer deserves to be paid, and Scripture affirms the support of those who labor in the word. There is no virtue in underpaying the people who serve the church, and much churches do it shamefully. But the professionalization of ministry carries a theological cost that the budget makes visible. When a large portion of the budget funds paid professionals to do the ministry, the budget is quietly confessing a theology in which ministry is done by experts on behalf of a paying congregation, rather than by the whole body of the priesthood of believers.

The budget, in other words, can either reinforce or resist the passivity of the laity. A staffing structure that hires professionals to do everything the members should be doing themselves is not neutral; it embodies a particular and questionable ecclesiology. A church that invests instead in equipping and releasing its members for ministry, that spends its resources multiplying ministers rather than employing them, embodies a different and more biblical vision. The staffing line is not just an administrative decision. It is a statement about who the church believes is called to do the work of the ministry.

## The Missing Line

Perhaps the most theologically revealing thing about a church budget is not what is in it but what is missing or minimal. Look for the line for the poor. Look for the line for those outside the walls. Look for the percentage that leaves the congregation to serve people who will never attend, never give, never contribute to the institution's survival. In many church budgets, this line is small, a token, a rounding error compared to the vast sums spent on the church's own comfort and continuation. And that smallness is a confession. It confesses a church curved inward, spending its resources on its own life while the poor at its gate receive the leftovers.

The prophets measured the faithfulness of Israel's worship by its treatment of the poor, and they found the elaborate religious spending worthless when it coexisted with neglect of the vulnerable. The same measure applies to a church budget. A congregation can have beautiful facilities, excellent programs, well-paid staff, and a budget that testifies against it before God because it spends everything on itself and almost nothing on the least of these. The size of the mercy line relative to the comfort lines is one of the truest measures of a church's actual theology, and it is a measure most churches would rather not take.

## Reading the Budget Rightly

What would it mean to treat the budget as the theological document it is? It would mean the leadership examining every line as a statement of belief and asking whether the spending matches the stated mission. It would mean the congregation being invited to see the budget not as a boring financial report but as a corporate confession of faith, open to examination and repentance. It would mean asking, honestly and painfully, whether the pattern of the church's spending would be recognizable to the church of Acts, or whether we have built something that spends on itself what the early church spent on the poor and the lost.

## The Budget and the Watching World

There is an evangelistic dimension to the church budget that we rarely consider, and it emerges from the way the early church's economic life functioned as its most powerful witness. The pagan world around the first Christians was struck not primarily by their doctrines, which most outsiders found strange, but by their behavior, and specifically by how they used their money. They cared for their own poor and for the poor outside their community. They buried the destitute. They took in abandoned infants. During plagues, when others fled, they stayed and nursed the sick, often dying in the process. The Emperor Julian, who despised Christianity and tried to revive paganism, complained bitterly that the Christians cared not only for their own poor but for the pagan poor as well, and that this generosity was winning converts his own religion could not match.

The economic life of the church was its apologetic. A budget that pours out resources on the vulnerable, that visibly loves the poor and the stranger, preaches the gospel to a watching world in a way no advertising campaign can. And a budget that spends everything on the comfort of its own members preaches a different message entirely, that this church is a club for its own benefit, indistinguishable from any other organization that exists to serve its members. The world is watching what the church does with its money, whether the church realizes it or not, and the budget is a sermon addressed as much to the neighborhood as to the congregation.

## Small Budgets, Faithful Churches

None of this should be heard as a rebuke reserved for large, wealthy churches. A small church with a modest budget faces exactly the same theological questions, and often answers them more faithfully than the megachurch with its enormous resources. The question is never the size of the budget but its proportions and its heart. A tiny congregation that gives sacrificially to the poor from its small offerings is preaching a truer sermon than a wealthy church that gives a token from its abundance. The widow's two coins, Jesus said, were worth more than all the large sums the rich threw into the treasury, because she gave out of her poverty everything she had, while they gave out of their wealth what they would not miss.

This is liberating for the small church, which often labors under a sense of inadequacy about its limited resources. Your budget is small, but it can be faithful, and faithfulness is what God measures. A small budget stewarded toward the poor, toward mission, toward the equipping of the saints, is a beautiful theological document, whatever its total. The question the budget poses is the same for the church of thirty and the church of three thousand: does the way we spend our money look like the heart of Jesus, or does it look like the heart of every other institution that exists to perpetuate and comfort itself?

## The Congregation That Never Sees It

One reason the budget fails to function as the theological document it is comes down to a simple problem of access: most members of most churches never actually look at it. The budget is prepared by a committee, approved in a sparsely attended meeting, and filed away, and the average member has no idea how their church's money is actually spent. They give, and the giving disappears into a black box, and the theological confession the budget makes goes unread by the very people whose gifts compose it. This is a lost opportunity, and arguably a form of poor stewardship of the congregation's own discipleship.

Imagine instead a church that treated its budget as an instrument of formation, that walked its members through where the money goes, that explained the theological reasoning behind its priorities, that invited the congregation to see their collective giving as a corporate act of worship with a visible shape. Such transparency would do more than satisfy accountability; it would disciple. It would teach the congregation, concretely, what it means for a community to hold money faithfully, to prioritize the poor, to fund mission, to resist the gravitational pull toward self-comfort. The budget is a sermon, and a church that hides it from its own people has muted one of the clearest sermons it preaches. To bring the budget into the light is to let the congregation see, and be shaped by, the theology their giving actually expresses.

## Repentance in Numbers

The most hopeful thing about seeing the budget as theology is that a budget can be changed, and changing it is one of the most concrete forms of corporate repentance a church can perform. Most repentance is invisible and internal; it happens in hearts and is known only to God. But budgetary repentance is visible, measurable, and real. When a church moves a significant portion of its spending from its own comfort to the service of the poor, from the maintenance of its building to the equipping of its people, from perpetuating the institution to reaching those outside it, something has genuinely changed, and it can be seen in black and white.

This is why the budget is such a searching test. Words are cheap; a church can confess any priority it likes in its mission statement. But to actually move the money is to actually repent, to align the treasure with the confessed heart, to make the sermon the budget preaches finally match the sermon the pulpit preaches. I say this to my own congregation and to myself, because it is far easier to preach about the poor than to move the line in the budget that would actually serve them. Show me your budget, and I will show you your theology. And if the two do not match, it is the budget, not the statement of faith, that tells the truth.

chapters.title: The Ethics of Wealth Accumulation
chapters.summary: At what point does saving become hoarding, prudence become greed, security become idolatry? The Bible refuses to give us a number, and its refusal is itself the most important thing it says.
chapters.body:
Every thoughtful Christian who has any measure of financial success eventually arrives at an uncomfortable question, and the question does not have a clean answer. How much is too much? At what point does responsible saving cross the line into hoarding? When does prudent provision for the future become the barn-building of the rich fool? Where is the boundary between wise stewardship and the idolatry of wealth? We want a number. We want a threshold, a percentage, a net worth above which accumulation becomes sin. And the Bible, maddeningly and deliberately, refuses to give us one.

I have come to believe that this refusal is not an oversight but a mercy, and that the absence of a clear line is itself the most important thing Scripture says on the subject. Because the moment there is a line, the question becomes legal rather than spiritual, am I over the limit or under it, and the heart escapes examination entirely. The person just under the threshold feels righteous; the person just over it feels condemned; and neither has actually confronted the condition of their own soul. By refusing to draw the line, the Bible keeps the question where it belongs: not in the account balance but in the heart.

## The Case for Saving

Let us be fair to the affirmations first, because Scripture genuinely commends provision and does not romanticize poverty. Proverbs praises the ant who stores food in summer against the coming winter, and holds up foresight as wisdom against the folly of the person who consumes everything today with no thought for tomorrow. "The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." Providing for one's family is not merely permitted but commanded; failing to provide for your own household is described as a denial of the faith, worse than unbelief. Leaving an inheritance for one's children's children is spoken of as the mark of a good person. There is no biblical virtue in improvidence, in reckless consumption, in refusing to prepare for the future.

So the ascetic answer, that the truly spiritual give away everything and keep nothing, cannot be sustained from Scripture as a universal rule. There were wealthy believers throughout the biblical narrative who were not commanded to divest: Abraham, Job, Joseph of Arimathea, Lydia, the women who supported Jesus out of their means. Wealth is not per se sinful, and the accumulation of resources for legitimate purposes, provision, preparation, generosity, the funding of good work, is not condemned. The person who saves diligently and provides responsibly is not automatically a hoarder. This must be said clearly, because there is a false guilt that afflicts conscientious savers and it is not from God.

## The Case Against Accumulation

And yet the warnings against wealth in Scripture are so frequent, so severe, and so pointed that no honest reader can walk away comfortable. The rich fool builds bigger barns and dies that night, condemned not for any crime but for storing up treasure for himself while being poor toward God. The rich young ruler cannot follow Jesus because he cannot let go of his possessions. The rich man in the parable of Lazarus ends in torment, apparently for no sin more specific than enjoying his wealth while a beggar starved at his gate. "Woe to you who are rich," Jesus says, without qualification. "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." "You cannot serve both God and money."

> The Bible commends the ant who stores for winter and condemns the fool who builds bigger barns, and the difference between them is not the size of the storehouse. It is the posture of the heart that fills it.

Notice that the rich fool did exactly what the prudent ant did, he stored up against the future. The behavior was identical. What differed was the heart. The ant stored to survive; the fool stored to secure himself against ever needing anyone, including God, so he could say to his soul, take your ease, you have enough for many years. The same act of accumulation was wisdom in one and idolatry in the other, and the only difference was what the accumulation meant to the one doing it. This is precisely why there is no number. The line is not drawn in dollars. It is drawn in the heart, and the heart cannot be measured externally.

## The Diagnostic Questions

If there is no threshold, how does a person examine themselves? The Bible offers not a number but a set of diagnostic questions, and they cut deeper than any accounting rule. The first is a question of function: what is your wealth for? Is it a tool held loosely for provision and generosity, or is it a fortress built to make you independent of God and indifferent to your neighbor? The rich fool's wealth had become a fortress. He wanted enough to never need anything again, and that desire, to be self-sufficient, to be secure apart from God, is the root of the idolatry. Wealth held as a tool is stewardship; wealth held as security is idolatry, and the same amount can be either.

The second is a question of grip: could you let it go? The rich young ruler's problem was revealed the moment Jesus asked him to release what he had. He could not. The wealth had him more than he had it. This is the test Jesus applied, and it is a fearful one, because most of us do not know whether we could let go until we are asked, and by then our answer reveals what has quietly become our master. The person who could cheerfully give it all away if God asked holds their wealth rightly, whatever its size. The person who could not is enslaved, whatever its size.

The third is a question of neighbor: does your accumulation coexist with indifference to the poor? The rich man in the Lazarus parable is condemned in a context where a beggar was starving at his very gate. His sin was not that he was rich but that he was rich while a man died in his sight and he did nothing. Accumulation that leaves you blind to need, that builds your comfort while ignoring the suffering within your reach, has crossed from stewardship into the very thing the prophets denounced. The question is not only how much you have but whom you have failed to see while you had it.

## The Trajectory Question

There is a fourth diagnostic, and it is perhaps the most practically useful: what is the trajectory of your accumulation? Is your wealth increasing so that your generosity can increase, or is it increasing so that your lifestyle can increase without end? Randy Alcorn calls this the difference between a rising standard of living and a rising standard of giving. The problem with wealth accumulation for most of us is not that we save but that every increase in income becomes an increase in consumption, a bigger house, a nicer car, a more expensive life, with the giving staying flat or shrinking as a percentage. The accumulation feeds the self endlessly, and there is never a point of enough.

The Christian who has settled a ceiling on their own consumption, who has decided that beyond a certain point, additional income flows not to more lifestyle but to more generosity, has found a way to accumulate without being consumed by accumulation. The wealth increases, but it increases as a river passing through rather than a reservoir filling up. This is not a rule that fits everyone identically, but it is a posture that guards the heart, because it breaks the automatic link between having more and spending more on oneself that drives the whole engine of greed.

## Living Without the Line

So we are left without the number we wanted, and I have come to be grateful for its absence. If there were a line, I would spend my life hovering just beneath it, congratulating myself on my restraint while my heart quietly worshiped what I was permitted to keep. The absence of a line forces me to a harder and more honest work: examining not my balance but my grip, not my net worth but my trajectory, not whether I am under some threshold but whether the God I claim to serve or the money I actually serve is Lord of what I have.

## The Comparison That Deceives

The single greatest obstacle to honest self-examination about wealth is the reflex to compare upward, and it deserves special attention because it disables the whole diagnostic before it can begin. Every wealthy person knows someone wealthier. The millionaire looks at the billionaire and feels modest. The person with two homes looks at the person with five and feels restrained. This upward comparison is nearly universal and nearly always self-serving, because it always positions the rich warnings of Scripture as being about someone else, the person one rung higher, and never about oneself.

The correction is to compare not upward but outward and backward. Compared to the global poor, to the billions who live on almost nothing, most of us reading this are staggeringly wealthy. Compared to nearly every human being who has ever lived before the modern age, we possess comforts and securities that kings could not command. When you compare across the whole human family rather than up the narrow ladder of your own affluent context, the warnings of Scripture about the rich stop being about someone else and land squarely on you. The rich man in the Lazarus parable was not the wealthiest man in the world. He was simply a man with more than enough while a poor man starved nearby. By that measure, the warning is for most of us, and the upward comparison that exempts us is one of the most effective lies the idol tells.

## The Freedom on the Other Side

It would be a distortion to leave the impression that this whole subject is only warning and self-suspicion, because on the far side of the searching questions lies a genuine freedom, and it is the freedom Jesus was actually offering the rich young ruler when he told him to sell what he had. The invitation was not merely a test or a burden; it was an offer of liberation from a master that was strangling him. Jesus looked at him and loved him, the text says, and then offered him the way out of the fortress he had built around himself. The man could not take it, and he went away sorrowful, still rich and still enslaved.

The person who holds wealth with a truly open hand, who could let it go, who has not made it a fortress, who sees the poor and gives freely, whose accumulation flows outward, has found something the anxious accumulator never will: rest. They are free from the exhausting vigilance of the person who must guard and grow and protect an ever-larger pile. They can enjoy what they have without clutching it, provide without hoarding, plan without idolizing. This is the freedom the gospel offers on the other side of the hard questions, and it is worth every discomfort the questions cost. The point of the examination is not to make the wealthy miserable but to make them free.

## The Enjoyment of Good Gifts

Lest the whole subject collapse into anxious self-suspicion, Scripture insists on a counterweight that the guilt-ridden Christian tends to forget: God gives us good things to enjoy. Paul, in the very passage where he commands the rich to be generous and warns against hoarding, first says that God richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment. Ecclesiastes repeatedly commends eating your bread with joy and drinking your wine with a merry heart, receiving the good of your labor as a gift from God's hand. The material world is not evil, and enjoying its goods with gratitude is not greed. The God who made a world of abundance did not intend his people to receive it with guilt.

This matters because a certain kind of scrupulous Christian, having heard all the warnings about wealth, tips into a joyless asceticism in which every pleasure is suspect and every enjoyment a compromise. That is not the biblical vision either. The line between grateful enjoyment and idolatrous indulgence is not always easy to draw, but the difference in spirit is real. The one receives good gifts with open, thankful hands, holding them loosely, ready to share, unattached; the other clutches them, defines itself by them, cannot imagine life without them. Enjoyment held in gratitude and open-handedness is a form of worship. It is only when the gift becomes the god, when the enjoyment becomes an attachment, that it curdles into the idolatry the warnings address. The wealthy Christian is called neither to guilt nor to greed but to grateful, generous, open-handed enjoyment of a good world given by a generous God.

I write this as someone genuinely wealthy by any global or historical measure, and the temptation to aim these questions at someone richer is constant and revealing. The ethics of wealth accumulation are not for the billionaire down the road. They are for me, holding what I hold, asking whether I could let it go, whether it has become my fortress, whether I have grown blind to the Lazarus at my gate, whether my abundance flows outward or only inward. The Bible will not tell me how much is too much. It tells me to look at my own heart, honestly, and to keep looking, because the idol of wealth hides best in the person most confident they are free of it. There is no number. There is only the daily, searching question, and the mercy that it has no easy answer.

chapters.title: The Wealth Gap and the Church
chapters.summary: The chasm between rich and poor has widened into something the prophets would have recognized instantly and denounced without hesitation. The church's silence is not neutrality. It is a position.
chapters.body:
We live in a time of staggering economic inequality, and most churches have decided to say nothing about it. The wealthiest fraction of the population controls a share of the resources that would have been unimaginable to previous generations, while millions work full-time and cannot afford a place to live. This is not a marginal feature of the economy. It is one of the defining facts of our age. And in the face of it, the vast majority of pulpits are quiet, not because the Bible is quiet, but because we have decided that the subject is political, and political means dangerous, and dangerous means we would rather preach about something else.

I want to argue that this silence is itself a theological position, and a bad one. The prophets were not silent about the gap between rich and poor. Jesus was not silent. The early church was not silent. When the modern church chooses silence, it is not staying neutral. It is siding, by default, with the arrangement as it stands. And that is a choice the Scriptures will not let us make comfortably.

## The Prophets Would Recognize This Instantly

Read Amos, Micah, and Isaiah with the newspaper open beside you and the resonance is uncanny. The prophets addressed a specific historical situation: eighth-century Israel and Judah were experiencing tremendous economic growth, and the fruits of that growth were flowing overwhelmingly to a wealthy elite while the small farmers were being pushed off their land, loaded with debt, and reduced to servitude. The rich were not necessarily breaking the letter of the law. They were manipulating the system, seizing fields, rigging the courts, tilting the scales, in ways that were technically defensible and morally monstrous.

Micah names it exactly: "They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them. They defraud people of their homes, they rob them of their inheritance." Isaiah names it: "Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field till no space is left and you live alone in the land." The word woe is not a policy critique. It is a funeral cry. The prophets were pronouncing death over an economic arrangement that concentrated wealth by dispossessing the vulnerable, and they were doing it in the name of God, to a people who considered themselves faithful.

> The prophets never once suggested that private wealth was neutral while public sin was the only real problem. They treated the concentration of wealth as itself a form of violence against the poor.

This is the piece we most want to avoid. We are comfortable condemning theft, fraud, individual greed, sins that can be pinned on bad individuals. The prophets went further. They condemned systems. They indicted an entire economic order that produced injustice through mechanisms no single person controlled, and they held the whole society, especially its beneficiaries, responsible for it. That kind of critique makes us deeply uncomfortable, and it should, because most of us reading this are the beneficiaries.

## The Structural and the Personal

Here is where the conversation usually splits into two camps that talk past each other. One camp says the problem is personal: individuals need to be generous, greed is a sin of the heart, and if enough people were converted the economic problems would take care of themselves. The other camp says the problem is structural: the systems themselves are unjust, and personal generosity is a bandage on a wound that requires surgery. Each camp accuses the other of missing the point, and each is half right.

The Bible refuses to choose. It holds the personal and the structural together in a way that neither modern camp manages. The prophets condemned personal greed and unjust systems in the same breath, because they understood that systems are built and maintained by people, and that people are shaped and tempted by systems. There is no clean separation. The wealthy individual who gives generously while benefiting from and defending an unjust arrangement has not answered the prophetic critique with his charity. And the reformer who fights for just structures while nursing a hard and grasping heart has not answered it either. The Bible wants both the heart and the system, and it will not let you use one to dodge the other.

## The Church's Complicity

Now the hard part, the part that implicates me and the institution I serve. The church is not merely a bystander to economic inequality. In many cases it is a participant and a beneficiary. Consider how church communities often sort themselves by class, the wealthy suburban congregation and the struggling urban one worshiping the same God a few miles apart and almost never in the same room. Consider how the largest and most resourced churches are frequently found where the money already is, while the neighborhoods that most need ministry are the ones least able to sustain it. Consider how easily the American church has baptized the pursuit of wealth, blessed the accumulators, and left the poor to feel that their poverty is somehow a spiritual failure.

James, the brother of Jesus, wrote directly about this failure, and it is one of the most pointed passages in the New Testament. He describes a church that gives the wealthy visitor the good seat and tells the poor man in shabby clothes to stand or sit on the floor, and he calls it what it is: discrimination, judging with evil thoughts, dishonoring the poor whom God has chosen. The early church already had this problem, and James did not soften it. He did not say be nice to everyone. He said you have made distinctions that God does not make, you have honored what God honors least and shamed what God honors most, and you have done it inside the assembly of Christ.

## The God Who Sides with the Poor

There is a phrase that makes many comfortable Christians nervous, the preferential option for the poor, and it is worth confronting rather than dismissing. It does not mean God loves the poor more than the rich, or that poverty is virtue and wealth is vice. It means something the Scriptures state repeatedly and unmistakably: that God pays particular attention to the vulnerable, that he hears the cry of the oppressed, that he identifies himself especially with those whom the powerful ignore. "Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord." "He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker." Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah's announcement of good news to the poor, and he identified himself so completely with the least that he said what you did to them you did to him.

This is not a marginal theme you have to hunt for. It runs through the entire canon like a spine. And it means that a church that ignores the wealth gap is not merely neglecting a social issue. It is ignoring one of God's most consistent and passionate concerns. It is loving the God of the Bible while turning away from the very people that God has said he especially sees.

## What Faithfulness Requires

So what does faithfulness look like, short of the political prescriptions that would divide any congregation in half? It begins with refusing the silence. The pulpit must be willing to name what the prophets named, not with partisan solutions, but with prophetic honesty about the reality that the gap between rich and poor is a matter God cares about intensely, and that the beneficiaries of the gap, which is most of us, are implicated in it.

It continues with the church becoming a place where the class divide is actually crossed rather than reinforced, where rich and poor sit at the same table, share the same bread, know one another by name, and discover that the categories the world uses to sort people mean nothing at the foot of the cross. This is harder than writing a check to a poverty program, and it is the thing James actually demanded. A congregation that is economically homogeneous has, whether it means to or not, conformed to the world's sorting rather than the kingdom's.

And it requires personal reckoning from those of us who benefit. I am, by any global or historical standard, wealthy. The temptation is to hear the prophetic word about the wealth gap as a message for someone richer than I am, the billionaire, the executive, the person one rung up the ladder. That is the oldest evasion in the book, and I have used it. The word is for me. It asks what I am doing with what I have, whom I have failed to see, and whether my comfort has been built, in ways I have never bothered to examine, on an arrangement that leaves others out in the cold. The prophets did not let their hearers off with that question, and I cannot let myself off either.

## The Danger of the Political Escape Hatch

There is a move both sides of the political spectrum make to avoid the prophetic word, and it deserves to be named, because it is how comfortable Christians dodge the whole subject. The one side says the answer is entirely governmental, pass the right laws, redistribute through the state, and my personal responsibility is discharged by voting correctly. The other side says the answer is entirely personal and voluntary, charity, not policy, and any structural remedy is an intrusion on freedom. And here is the trick: each position becomes a way of doing nothing. The first outsources the obligation to the government so the individual heart is never touched. The second outsources it to a voluntary charity that somehow never quite happens at the scale required.

The prophetic word cuts through both escape hatches. It will not let the individual hide behind policy, and it will not let the defender of freedom hide behind a charity he never actually practices. It comes for the heart and the hands directly. Amos did not tell the wealthy of Israel to vote differently or to feel differently. He told them their behavior was crushing the poor and that God was going to hold them personally accountable for it. Whatever one concludes about the proper role of government in addressing inequality, and Christians of good faith will disagree, no political conclusion relieves the individual believer of the direct, personal, unavoidable obligation to see the poor, to open the hand, to refuse to build comfort on the backs of the vulnerable. The politics is a real question. It is not a hiding place.

## The Test of a Church

In the end, the wealth gap poses a test to the church that is finally simpler than all the policy debates, and it is the test James laid down: when the rich and the poor are both in the room, which one gets the good seat? A church reveals its true theology not in its statement of faith but in whom it honors, whom it centers, whom it is organized to serve. A church that has, without ever deciding to, become a comfortable club for the prosperous while the poor feel their poverty as shame the moment they walk in has failed the test, however orthodox its doctrine.

## The Comfort That Blinds

There is a specific spiritual danger that attends the beneficiaries of inequality, and it is not primarily cruelty. It is blindness. The rich man in the parable of Lazarus is not described as actively tormenting the beggar at his gate; his sin is that he did not see him, day after day, as he stepped over him on the way to his feasts. Comfort has a way of narrowing vision, of making the suffering of others recede into background scenery, of rendering the poor invisible precisely to those with the most power to help them. The wealthy do not have to hate the poor to fail them. They only have to stop seeing them, and comfort makes not-seeing effortless.

This is why the wealth gap is a spiritual problem for the comfortable and not merely a policy problem for the society. It is doing something to us, dulling our sight, insulating us from the reality of need, allowing us to live untroubled beside suffering we have trained ourselves not to notice. The gated community, the segregated neighborhood, the curated feed, the careful avoidance of the parts of town where poverty lives, these are the mechanisms by which the modern rich, myself included, keep from seeing the Lazarus at the gate. And the not-seeing is not innocent. It is the very sin the parable condemns. To recover sight, to deliberately place ourselves where we cannot avoid seeing the poor, to refuse the comfort that blinds, is a spiritual discipline the affluent Christian desperately needs and almost never practices.

The early church passed this test in a way that astonished the watching Roman world. Pagan observers noted with bewilderment that these Christians cared for each other across every social line, that the wealthy shared with the poor, that widows and orphans and the destitute were absorbed into a community that treated them as family. It was one of the most compelling apologetics the early church possessed, not an argument but a demonstration, a community in which the wealth gap that structured the whole ancient world simply did not determine who mattered. The gap is real. God sees it. And the church's silence has gone on long enough. It is time we became again the community that the gap cannot divide.

chapters.title: Tithing: Command, Principle, or Guilt Trip?
chapters.summary: The ten percent has become a Christian shibboleth few can defend from the New Testament and most give reluctantly. The truth is stranger and more demanding than the number.
chapters.body:
Somewhere in the life of nearly every churchgoing Christian there is a low-grade, chronic guilt about the tithe. You know the number, ten percent, and you know you are probably not hitting it, and you know the pastor is going to preach on stewardship sometime around the fall budget season, and you brace for it the way you brace for a dentist appointment. The tithe has become one of the great sources of ambient shame in the Christian financial imagination. And the strange thing is that almost no one can actually tell you where the ten percent comes from, whether it is binding, or what it is supposed to mean.

So let us do the thing the guilt prevents us from doing. Let us actually look at what the Bible says about the tithe, and let us be honest about where the conventional teaching is standing on solid ground and where it is standing on nothing at all.

## The Old Testament Tithe Was Not What You Think

Start with the surprise. The tithe in the Old Testament was not a single ten percent. It was a system of multiple tithes that, taken together, amounted to something closer to twenty or twenty-three percent of annual produce. There was the Levitical tithe that supported the priestly tribe who had no land inheritance. There was the festival tithe that funded the annual pilgrimages and feasts. And there was a third-year tithe stored in the towns to feed the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the Levite. The tithe was fundamentally agricultural, tied to the produce of the land and the increase of the flocks, and it functioned as something like a combined religious tax and social welfare system for the covenant nation.

This complicates the modern sermon considerably. When a pastor stands up and says "the Bible commands you to tithe ten percent of your income," he is compressing a complex, multi-layered agricultural system into a single number and applying it to a wage economy the Torah never envisioned. That does not make the compression illegitimate, but it should make the preacher humble about how directly he can wield the word command. I have preached the ten percent as though it fell from heaven with a decimal point already attached. It did not.

## Abraham and Jacob: Before the Law

The tithe predates the law of Moses, which is the strongest argument that it reflects something more permanent than the Sinai covenant. Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek in Genesis 14, a spontaneous act of worship after a military victory, long before there was any commandment requiring it. Jacob, fleeing his brother, vowed at Bethel that if God brought him home safely he would give God a tenth of everything.

These two episodes are the favorite proof texts of the pro-tithing preacher, and they carry real weight, but notice what they actually show. Both are voluntary. Both are responses to grace already received, Abraham to victory, Jacob to a promise. Neither is a religious tax paid under obligation. They establish that giving God a proportion of what you have is an ancient instinct of worship. They do not establish that the proportion is legally fixed at ten percent for all people in all times.

## Jesus and the Tithe

Here is the text that gets left out of the stewardship sermon. In Matthew 23, Jesus rebukes the Pharisees: "You give a tenth of your spices, mint, dill and cumin. But you have neglected the more important matters of the law, justice, mercy and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former." This is the only place Jesus directly addresses the tithe, and it is a stunning statement. He affirms the tithe, you should have practiced the former, while making clear that it is the least of the commandments, a matter so minor that a person can scrupulously obey it while missing the entire point of the law.

> The Pharisees tithed their herb garden and swallowed injustice whole. Jesus did not tell them to stop tithing. He told them the tithe had become a way of not loving anyone.

This is the danger the tithe carries, and it is a danger I have watched play out in my own congregation and my own heart. The number becomes a ceiling instead of a floor. You write the check, you cross the line, you feel the small warm glow of obligation discharged, and you close your hand around the remaining ninety percent as though it were now entirely and unquestionably yours. But the New Testament nowhere teaches that ninety percent is yours. It teaches that one hundred percent is God's, and that you are a steward of all of it.

## The New Testament's Silence and Its Meaning

The most important fact about the tithe in the New Testament is how little it appears. Paul, who wrote more about money and giving than any other apostle, never once commands the tithe. When he takes up the great collection for Jerusalem in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, he does not say "remember your ten percent." He says something both freer and more terrifying: "Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." And in 1 Corinthians 16 he asks each person to set aside a sum in keeping with their income, proportional, but not fixed.

Some read this silence as liberation: the tithe is abolished, give whatever you feel like. But that reading gets the direction exactly backward. The New Testament does not lower the bar below the tithe. It removes the bar and replaces it with the whole of your life. Under the old covenant you owed ten percent and the rest was, in a sense, negotiable. Under the new covenant you owe everything, because you have been bought with a price and you are not your own. The tithe was a training-wheel proportion for a people learning to give. The gospel invites you off the training wheels into a generosity with no ceiling at all.

## So Should You Tithe?

Here is where I have landed after fifteen years of preaching this, and I offer it as a pastor rather than a lawyer. The ten percent is not a New Testament command, and any preacher who tells you it is has overstated his case. But it is an extraordinarily wise starting place. It is a proportion old enough to predate the law and specific enough to be actionable, and it forces a question that vaguer instructions let us dodge. If you tell people to give as their heart decides, most hearts will decide on very little, because the heart is an accomplished self-deceiver, and mine is the most accomplished of all.

So I teach the tithe not as law but as trellis, a structure to grow on. For the person who has never given systematically, ten percent is a bracing and clarifying goal that will reorder your finances and expose your idols faster than any sermon. For the person who has been giving faithfully for years, ten percent may be far too low, a comfortable plateau you have long since outgrown, and the honest question is not whether you are tithing but whether you are still being stretched.

## The Guilt Question

What about the guilt? The chronic, low-grade shame that the word tithe produces in so many faithful people? I want to name it directly, because I do not think it comes from God. Guilt that drives you toward generosity as an escape from condemnation is not gospel motivation; it is precisely the compulsion Paul rejects. God does not want your ten percent extracted from you by fear. He wants your heart, and the giving is meant to follow the heart, not manufacture it.

If you are giving out of guilt, the problem is not that you are giving too little. The problem is that you have not yet believed the gospel deeply enough to give freely. The cure is not a larger check written in the same spirit. The cure is to sit long enough under the fact that Christ became poor for you, that everything you have is already grace, that you cannot buy God's approval because it has already been given, until the check stops being a payment and becomes a thank-you. A person who truly believes she has received everything does not tithe reluctantly. She gives, and gives past the tithe, and wonders why she waited so long, and cannot imagine going back.

## The Malachi Problem

No conversation about tithing can avoid the one text that dominates every stewardship sermon: Malachi 3, where God says through the prophet, "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse. Test me in this, and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing that there will not be room enough to store it." This is the verse printed on the offering envelope, quoted from the platform, wielded as the clincher. And it is almost always misused.

Read in context, Malachi is addressing a specific covenant people under a specific covenant, accusing them of robbing God by withholding the tithes and offerings that supported the temple and the Levites. It is a national indictment of covenant unfaithfulness, not a universal formula for personal financial return. When it is ripped out of that context and turned into a promise that individual Christians who tithe will receive material blessing, it becomes a soft form of the prosperity gospel, give to get, tithe as investment strategy, God as the guarantor of your financial upside. That is not what Malachi teaches, and the preacher who uses it that way has traded the text's actual meaning for a fundraising slogan. God is not a vending machine, and the tithe is not a coin you insert to trigger a payout.

This does not empty Malachi of meaning. It genuinely does indict the withholding heart, the heart that clutches what belongs to God and calls it prudence. But the blessing Malachi promises is covenant faithfulness restored, not a guaranteed return on a religious investment. I have preached this verse badly, leaning on its promise of overflow because it moved people to give, and in doing so I taught them to give for the wrong reason and to expect the wrong reward. The honest use of Malachi confronts the robbery without promising the payout.

## Giving as Warfare Against the Self

Underneath the whole tithing debate lies a truth that both sides tend to miss: the primary beneficiary of your giving is not the church. It is you. Giving is spiritual warfare against the most stubborn enemy you will ever face, which is your own grasping heart. Every time you release money that your instincts scream at you to keep, you strike a blow against the idol of mammon that wants to rule you. The tithe, whatever its precise status as command or principle, is training in that warfare, a disciplined, repeated act of loosening your grip on the thing you most want to hold.

This is why the question is finally not whether the ten percent is legally binding but whether you are being changed. A person can give the exact tithe for forty years and remain as tightfisted and anxious as the day they started, because the giving never touched the heart. And a person can give with such freedom and joy that the money means nothing next to the God who gave it all. The number is a starting place. The transformation is the point. Give, then, begin with the tithe if you have no better starting place, but give in order to be freed, and keep giving until the day comes when you cannot remember why you ever found it hard.

## Where the Money Goes

A question that the tithing debate usually neglects is where the tithe should actually go, and it matters more than we admit. The default assumption in most churches is that the tithe belongs entirely to the local congregation, that giving to the church budget is what tithing means. But the Old Testament tithe supported not only the religious institution but the poor, the foreigner, the vulnerable. The third-year tithe was specifically for the destitute. To reduce the tithe to funding the local church's budget, much of which goes to buildings and staff, is to narrow something that Scripture kept broad.

This does not mean you should stop supporting your church, which needs resources to do its work. It means the biblical vision of proportional giving was always wider than the offering plate, encompassing the poor, the work of mission, the care of the vulnerable, and that a healthy giving life reflects that breadth. The person who gives faithfully to their church and never gives directly to the poor has captured only part of the picture. The tithe, in its fullest biblical sense, was always partly for the least of these, and our giving is impoverished when it forgets them.

## Teaching Children to Give

One of the most lasting things a parent can do about money is to teach their children to give before the culture teaches them to accumulate, and this is where the practical wisdom of the tithe becomes a gift rather than a burden. A child who learns early to set aside a portion of every gift and every earning for God and for others is being formed in a habit that will guard them for life against the grasping that captures almost everyone else. The specific proportion matters less than the pattern: giving first, giving regularly, giving as a normal and joyful part of how one relates to money.

I have watched this formation take root, and I have watched its absence. The child raised to give grows into an adult for whom generosity is second nature, who does not have to overcome a lifetime of accumulation to open their hand. The child raised only to save and spend grows into an adult who finds giving painful and unnatural, who must fight against decades of formation every time they release a dollar. If the tithe is finally a trellis for growing generous people, there is no better time to set up the trellis than in childhood, when the vine is young and can be trained toward open hands from the start.

chapters.title: Treasures in Heaven
chapters.summary: Jesus told us to store up treasures in heaven, and we have quietly filed this away as poetic and impractical. But he meant it as an actual investment strategy, the only one that survives death.
chapters.body:
Jesus said something about money that we have almost entirely failed to take literally. "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moths and vermin destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moths and vermin do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." We treat this as beautiful poetry, a nice sentiment about not being too materialistic, a general encouragement toward spiritual-mindedness. And in treating it that way, we have missed that Jesus was giving concrete financial instruction. He was describing an actual investment strategy, and claiming it was the only one that ultimately made sense.

The passage is not vague spirituality. It is a comparison of two portfolios, and a recommendation to move your assets from one to the other. Jesus, the master teacher, was making an argument that any investor should recognize: one of these investments is guaranteed to be destroyed, and the other is guaranteed to last forever, so you would be a fool to keep your treasure in the perishable one. The strangeness is not that he used financial language. The strangeness is that we have refused to believe he meant it.

## The Argument from Permanence

Follow the logic Jesus actually lays out, because it is more rigorous than we give it credit for. Earthly treasure, he says, is subject to three threats: moth, rust, and theft. In his agrarern context, wealth was stored as fine cloth that moths ate, as metal goods that corroded, as valuables that thieves stole. His point was that all earthly treasure is, by its nature, perishable and vulnerable. It decays, it corrodes, it can be taken, and even if none of these befall it in your lifetime, death will separate you from it completely. No earthly treasure survives your own death. Every dollar you accumulate, you will leave behind. The hearse does not pull a trailer.

Heavenly treasure, by contrast, is immune to all three threats. It does not decay, cannot be stolen, and is not lost at death, indeed, it is precisely what death delivers you into. Jesus is making an argument from permanence, and it is unanswerable on its own terms. If you have a choice between investing in something guaranteed to be destroyed and something guaranteed to last forever, and if you are going to exist forever, then the rational choice is obvious. To pour your life into accumulating what you cannot keep, while neglecting to accumulate what you cannot lose, is not merely unspiritual. It is, by Jesus' logic, foolish. It is bad investing.

> Jesus was not being poetic. He was being practical. He looked at your portfolio and said: you are heavily invested in an asset guaranteed to be destroyed. Move your money.

## What Heavenly Treasure Is

The natural question is what, exactly, treasure in heaven consists of, and how one actually stores it up. Jesus and the apostles give surprisingly concrete answers. In Luke, immediately after telling the parable of the rich fool, Jesus says: "Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide purses for yourselves that will not wear out, a treasure in heaven that will never fail." Storing treasure in heaven is directly linked to generosity toward the poor. The act of giving away earthly wealth is the mechanism by which heavenly wealth is accumulated. You transfer your treasure from the perishable account to the imperishable one by giving it away, a transaction that looks like loss to the world and is actually the shrewdest possible investment.

Paul makes the same connection explicit in his instructions to the rich, and it is one of the most remarkable passages in Scripture on this theme. Command those who are rich, he says, to be generous and willing to share, and in this way they will "lay up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life." The generous use of wealth is described as an investment that stores up treasure for the age to come. This is not metaphor stacked on metaphor. It is a claim about the actual mechanics of eternal reward: what you give away for the sake of Christ and his kingdom is not lost but transferred, laid up, stored where it cannot be destroyed, waiting for you.

## The Heart Follows the Treasure

There is a further dimension to this teaching that is easy to miss, and it concerns the direction of causation between treasure and heart. "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." Notice that Jesus does not say where your heart is, there your treasure will be. He says the reverse. Your heart follows your treasure. This is a profound observation about human nature: we come to love what we invest in. The things we pour our resources into become the things we care about. If you invest heavily in earthly things, your heart will be bound to earth. If you invest in heavenly things, your heart will be drawn toward heaven.

This means that generosity is not only a way of storing up eternal reward; it is a way of reorienting your own heart. When you give to the kingdom, your heart follows the gift, and you find yourself caring more about the kingdom, more about the poor you have invested in, more about the eternal things your treasure is now accumulating. The person who wants to love God and the things of God more deeply has a concrete tool available: move your treasure there, and your heart will follow. Generosity is heart-surgery you perform on yourself, redirecting your affections by redirecting your investments. This is why the miser is trapped and the giver is free, the miser's heart is chained to what he clutches, while the giver's heart is drawn upward toward what he has sent ahead.

## The Only Investment That Survives Death

What makes this teaching so urgent is the one fact we spend our whole lives avoiding: we are going to die, and death is the great liquidator of every earthly portfolio. The wealthiest person who ever lived left it all behind. The most successful career ends in a coffin. Every earthly treasure, no matter how carefully accumulated and guarded, is confiscated in full at the moment of death, and we take nothing with us. This is not morbid; it is simply true, and Jesus builds his entire argument on it. In light of certain death, an investment strategy that only pays off before death is a strategy with a guaranteed total loss at the end.

Treasure in heaven is the only investment that survives the one event that liquidates everything else. What you give away for Christ does not die when you die; it is waiting for you on the other side. This reframes the whole logic of accumulation. The person storing up earthly wealth is investing everything in an account that will be zeroed out at death. The person storing up heavenly treasure through generosity is investing in the only account that death cannot touch, that in fact matures at death. Seen clearly, generosity is not the sacrifice of wealth; it is the transfer of wealth from the account that dies to the account that lives forever. The giver is not the one losing money. The hoarder is.

## Believing It Enough to Do It

The reason we do not live this way is not that we disagree with Jesus' argument; it is that we do not really believe it, not down in the places where our checkbooks are decided. We nod at the teaching on Sunday and invest in the perishable account on Monday, hedging our bets, treating the heavenly treasure as a nice hope while treating the earthly treasure as the real thing. Our spending reveals what we actually believe, and most of our spending confesses a functional unbelief in the very thing Jesus said was the only sound investment. I include myself in this indictment fully; my own account balances testify against my stated theology more days than not.

## The Shrewd Manager

There is a parable of Jesus so strange that most preachers avoid it entirely, and it turns out to be one of the clearest illustrations of the treasures-in-heaven principle in all his teaching. In Luke 16, a dishonest manager, about to be fired, uses his last days of authority to slash the debts owed to his master, currying favor with the debtors so they will welcome him after he loses his job. And astonishingly, the master commends the dishonest manager for acting shrewdly. Jesus then draws the lesson: use worldly wealth to gain friends for yourselves, so that when it is gone, you will be welcomed into eternal dwellings.

The point is not that we should imitate the man's dishonesty but that we should imitate his shrewdness, his clear-eyed recognition that his current position was temporary and his use of present resources to secure a future beyond it. He understood that the wealth in his hands was about to be lost, and he leveraged it, while he still had it, to secure a welcome on the other side. This is exactly the treasures-in-heaven logic. Our earthly wealth is temporary; we are about to lose it all at death; and the shrewd thing to do is to use it now, while we have it, to secure friends and welcome and reward in the eternal home that awaits us. Jesus is calling us to be as shrewd about eternity as the dishonest manager was about his unemployment, to see clearly that the money will not last and to invest it accordingly.

## What We Send Ahead

There is a moving way the older Christian tradition sometimes spoke about this, drawn from the missionary Jim Elliot and echoing ancient wisdom: the only things we truly keep are the things we give away, because what we hold we lose at death, and what we give for Christ we send ahead where it waits for us. This inverts the entire common-sense understanding of possession. We think we possess what we cling to and lose what we release. Jesus says the reverse: we lose what we cling to, because death confiscates it, and we keep what we release for his sake, because it is stored where death cannot reach.

This means the generous person is not depleting their estate but transferring it, moving their wealth, piece by piece, from the account that will be zeroed out to the account that will be waiting. Every gift to the poor, every resource poured into the kingdom, every dollar released for Christ is not gone but relocated, sent ahead to a home we have not yet reached but will not leave. The hoarder, who feels so secure behind their accumulated pile, is the one actually losing everything, because none of it will cross the threshold of death with them. The giver, who looks to the world like they are throwing wealth away, is the shrewdest investor of all, quietly building a treasure in the one place the universe cannot take it from them.

## The Eye and the Heart

In the middle of the treasures passage, Jesus says something that seems, at first, like a strange non sequitur: "The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are healthy, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eyes are unhealthy, your whole body will be full of darkness." Placed between the teaching about treasure and the declaration that you cannot serve two masters, this saying is not a digression; it is the hinge. In the idiom of Jesus' day, a good eye meant a generous person and a bad eye meant a stingy, grasping one. He is saying that the way you see, your fundamental orientation toward money and possession, determines whether your whole life is filled with light or darkness.

This is a profound observation about how money shapes perception. The grasping person, the one with the bad eye, does not merely have a financial problem; their entire vision of the world is darkened by their greed. They see other people as threats or resources, they see their possessions as extensions of themselves, they see the future as something to be secured against rather than trusted to God. The generous person, the one with the good eye, sees differently, sees others as neighbors to love, possessions as tools to deploy, the future as held by a faithful Father. Your relationship to money is not one compartment of your life among others; it is the lens through which you see everything, and it fills your whole existence with either light or darkness. This is why Jesus takes it so seriously. It is never just about money. It is about whether you can see at all.

## The Rich Man and the Regret

Jesus told a story about a rich man who died and found himself in torment, looking across an unbridgeable gulf at a poor man named Lazarus who had begged at his gate and was now comforted. The rich man's great desire, too late, was to warn his five brothers so they would not come to the same place. And the answer he received was that they had Moses and the prophets; if they would not listen to them, they would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead.

The story is a warning delivered from the far side of death, and its terror is precisely that the rich man cannot go back and reinvest. His portfolio is closed. The wealth he enjoyed in life, the fine clothes and sumptuous feasts, bought him nothing that lasted, and the poor man he ignored at his own gate turned out to be the one who mattered. The chance to store up treasure in heaven, to use his wealth to gain an eternal welcome, was available to him every single day, and he spent it all on himself, and now it is gone, and the regret is eternal. Jesus tells this story to the living, who still have time, whose portfolio is still open, who can still move their treasure while the market is open. The rich man cannot warn his brothers. But Jesus can, and does, and the warning is for us: the window in which you can send your treasure ahead is called your life, and it will not stay open forever.

To actually believe Jesus is to reorder the portfolio. It is to give generously not out of guilt or obligation but out of the shrewd recognition that this is the wisest possible use of resources that will otherwise be destroyed, to send treasure ahead where it cannot be lost, to store up what death cannot take, to invest in the age that does not end. Jesus was not asking us to be impractical for the sake of piety. He was inviting us to be more practical than the world, to see through the illusion that earthly treasure is the safe investment, and to put our money where it will still exist a thousand years from now. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. He told us where to send it. The only question is whether we believed him enough to do it.

chapters.title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
chapters.summary: The Bible neither baptizes wealth nor canonizes poverty, it treats money as a diagnostic instrument that reveals, with unbearable precision, what you actually worship.
chapters.body:
There are two popular versions of the Bible's teaching on money, and both of them are wrong. The first says God wants you rich, that faith is an investment strategy and the Almighty is a venture capitalist who rewards spiritual performance with material returns. The second says money is inherently corrupt, that genuine discipleship requires voluntary poverty, that wealth itself is the sin, and that any Christian who accumulates more than subsistence has already betrayed the gospel. The prosperity gospel and the poverty gospel stand on opposite street corners, shouting past each other, each holding a handful of proof texts and ignoring the rest of the canon.

The actual biblical witness is more demanding than either alternative. It does not condemn wealth. It does not promise it. It treats money as a diagnostic instrument, a tool of extraordinary precision for revealing what you actually worship. And it does this from the first book to the last, with a consistency that should unsettle anyone who has reduced the Bible's economic teaching to a bumper sticker.

## The Torah: Wealth as Covenant Gift

The economic theology of the Old Testament begins not with prohibition but with provision. Genesis 1 presents a God who creates abundance, a world teeming with life, resources distributed across the earth, human beings commissioned to cultivate and steward what has been given. The creation narrative is not ascetic. It does not regard the material world with suspicion. The refrain is not "be careful" but "it was good."

Deuteronomy 8 is the critical text, and it is almost never quoted in full by either side of the prosperity debate. Moses tells Israel that God is bringing them into a good land, a land with streams and springs, wheat and barley, olive oil and honey. "You will eat and be satisfied," he says, "and you will bless the Lord your God for the good land he has given you." This is unambiguous affirmation of material blessing. The prosperity preachers stop here. They should not.

The passage continues with a warning so severe it occupies more space than the promise: "Beware that you do not forget the Lord your God. When you have eaten and are satisfied, when you have built fine houses and settled down, when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all you have is multiplied, then your heart will become proud and you will forget the Lord your God." The danger is not wealth. The danger is the amnesia that wealth produces. You forget who gave it. You begin to believe your own hands produced it. And that forgetting is not a minor theological error. It is idolatry.

Craig Blomberg, in his exhaustive study *Neither Poverty nor Riches*, argues that the Torah's economic vision is structured around three interlocking principles: God owns everything, human beings are stewards of what has been entrusted, and the community bears collective responsibility for the vulnerable. The sabbatical year laws in Exodus 23 and Deuteronomy 15, requiring debt cancellation every seven years, are not charitable suggestions. They are structural provisions designed to prevent the permanent concentration of wealth. The jubilee legislation in Leviticus 25, mandating the return of ancestral land every fifty years, goes further still. Whether or not Israel ever fully practiced jubilee is debated among scholars, but its theological function is clear: the land belongs to God, you are tenants, and no family can be permanently dispossessed.

This is not socialism. It is not capitalism. It is a theocentric economy in which property rights are real but limited, wealth is permitted but monitored, and the accumulation of resources at the expense of the poor is treated as a direct offense against the God who owns the vineyard.

## The Prophets: Wealth as Indictment

If the Torah establishes the framework, the prophets enforce it. And they enforce it with a ferocity that should make every comfortable Western Christian deeply uneasy. Including me.

Amos, writing in the eighth century BC during a period of unprecedented Israelite prosperity under Jeroboam II, delivers the most sustained economic indictment in the Hebrew Bible. He does not attack wealth in the abstract. He names specific behaviors: selling the poor for a pair of sandals, trampling the heads of the needy, lying on beds of ivory while the nation crumbles. His targets are not pagans. They are the faithful, the people who attend the festivals, offer the sacrifices, sing the songs. "I hate, I despise your religious festivals," God says through Amos. "Away with the noise of your songs. But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream."

The prophetic critique is not that the wealthy are rich. It is that they are rich and religious simultaneously, that they have managed to worship God on the sabbath while exploiting the poor on Monday, and that they see no contradiction. Isaiah 58 makes the same point with devastating clarity: Israel asks why God does not respond to their fasting. God answers: because on the day of your fasting you exploit your workers. The worship is invalidated not by theological error but by economic behavior.

Justo Gonzalez, in *Faith and Wealth*, traces this prophetic thread through the intertestamental period and into the early church. He demonstrates that by the time of Jesus there existed a robust tradition, in the prophets, in the wisdom literature, in the apocalyptic writings, that linked economic justice to covenant fidelity. Jesus did not invent the connection between money and worship. He inherited it.

## Jesus: The Most Uncomfortable Teacher

Jesus talked about money more than he talked about heaven and hell combined. This is not a rhetorical exaggeration. It is a textual fact that anyone with a concordance can verify. And what he said was not comforting.

Luke 6 gives the version of the Beatitudes that prosperity preachers avoid. Matthew softens the language to "poor in spirit." Luke does not. "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort." There is no interpretive escape hatch here. The poor are blessed. The rich are warned. And the warning is not conditional, it does not say woe to you who are rich and also happen to be greedy. It says woe to you who are rich.

The parable of the rich fool in Luke 12 is aimed at a man who has done nothing illegal. He is a successful farmer. His land produces abundantly. He decides to build bigger barns and enjoy his retirement. He is, by every modern financial-planning standard, a model citizen. And God calls him a fool, not because he stole, not because he cheated, but because he stored up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God. The sin is a horizon that ends at the self.

Then there is the rich young ruler, who kept every commandment and still walked away sorrowful when Jesus told him to sell what he had and give to the poor. It is the only recorded instance of someone rejecting a direct invitation from Jesus and being permitted to leave. Jesus does not chase him. He watches him go and says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples are astonished, which tells you they had not yet learned to soften the saying the way we have.

> The Bible does not ask whether you have money. It asks whether your money has you. And that is a question the balance sheet cannot answer.

## The Early Church: A Community That Shared

Acts 2 and 4 describe a community in which no one claimed that any of their possessions was their own. They had everything in common. Those who owned land or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles, and it was distributed to anyone who had need. This was not enforced by law. Ananias and Sapphira were not judged for keeping their property but for lying about it, for pretending to a generosity they did not have. The problem was hypocrisy, not private ownership. But the direction of the community is unmistakable. The gravitational pull of the gospel is toward open hands.

Paul organized a collection across the Gentile churches for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, and in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 he laid out a theology of giving that has almost nothing in common with modern fundraising. He appeals to the Macedonians, who gave out of extreme poverty and severe affliction, and he grounds the whole enterprise in the self-emptying of Christ: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich. Generosity is not a technique. It is a participation in the movement of the incarnation.

## What This Means for a Tuesday Afternoon

I have preached on money for fifteen years, and I have watched my own heart flinch every time. It is easy to stand in a pulpit and denounce the rich when you have quietly decided that rich means the person with more than you. That is the oldest trick in the book, and I have used it. The prophetic word about wealth is not a weapon to aim at the people above you on the ladder. It is a mirror. It implicates the preacher first.

So here is the verdict, and it is not comfortable for me either. The Bible does not tell you how much money you are allowed to have. It tells you that whatever you have will testify against you or for you, and that the testimony will be economic before it is verbal. What you do with money is the most honest sermon you will ever preach. Your bank statement is a spiritual autobiography. It records, line by line, what you feared, what you loved, whom you forgot, and whom you saw.

You cannot serve God and money. Jesus said it plainly, and he used the word serve, which means slave. There is no arrangement in which both are masters. One will be Lord and the other will be tool. The question the Bible presses on every one of us, and it presses hardest on those of us who preach, is which is which. And you will not answer that question with your mouth. You will answer it with your checkbook, quietly, over the course of a life, and the answer will be true.

## The Wisdom Literature: Money Without Illusions

Between the Torah and the prophets sits a body of literature that treats money with an almost startling realism, and it is the part of the Bible most likely to disorient someone who has reduced the subject to a slogan. Proverbs praises diligence and warns against sloth; it commends the accumulation of resources through honest labor and treats poverty caused by laziness as folly. There is no romanticizing of destitution here.
