And yet the same book, sometimes on the same page, warns that the pursuit of riches is a snare, that the rich man's wealth is his imagined fortress, that a good name is worth more than great riches, and that the one who trusts in his wealth will fall.

Agur's prayer in Proverbs 30 is the wisdom tradition's most honest word on the subject, and it is almost never preached: "Give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread. Otherwise I may have too much and disown you and say, Who is the Lord? Or I may become poor and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God." Here is a man who understands that both wealth and want carry spiritual danger, that riches tempt toward self-sufficiency and forgetting God, while poverty tempts toward theft and despair. He asks for enough. Craig Blomberg titled his study after this prayer for good reason: neither poverty nor riches, but daily bread, is the wisdom tradition's answer to the money question, and it undercuts both the prosperity gospel and the poverty gospel at a single stroke.

Ecclesiastes goes further still, pressing on the futility of accumulation with a bleakness that most Christian teaching cannot bear. The Preacher has everything, wealth, projects, pleasure, achievement beyond any of his predecessors, and he finds it all vapor, a chasing after wind. He notices that he must leave everything to someone who did not work for it, and who may be a fool. He observes that the sleep of the laborer is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich permits him no sleep. This is not a rejection of work or wealth; the Preacher commends enjoying the fruit of one's labor as a gift from God. But it is a savage deflation of the idea that accumulation can satisfy. Money cannot fill the hole it promises to fill, and the wisdom literature says so with a candor the modern church rarely matches.

## James: The Prophet Returns

The letter of James picks up the prophetic thread and carries it directly into the church, refusing to let the New Testament soften the Old Testament's economic edge. James warns the rich who oppress their workers that the wages they have failed to pay are crying out, and that the cries have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty, an almost verbatim echo of the prophetic tradition. He rebukes the church for showing favoritism to the wealthy visitor and dishonoring the poor. He insists that faith without works is dead, and the works he has in mind are explicitly economic: clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, caring for widows and orphans in their distress.

James is the bridge that proves the economic teaching of the Bible is one continuous stream from Amos to the apostles. The gospel did not spiritualize away the concern for money and the poor; it intensified it. The community formed by the death and resurrection of Christ was to be marked, more than anything, by a radically different relationship to wealth, open-handed, generous, indifferent to status, oriented toward the vulnerable. Where the church has failed to be marked this way, it has not merely fallen short of an ideal. It has departed from the plain and consistent teaching of the book it claims to obey.

chapters.title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
chapters.summary: The Bible's first concern about money is not how much you have. It is what it is doing to you. Jesus named it mammon and treated it as a rival master.
chapters.body:
Jesus talked about money more than he talked about heaven, and far more than he talked about hell. By a common reckoning, about one of every ten verses in the Gospels touches it, and roughly a third of his parables turn on it. He came to deal with sin and death, and he spent a striking share of a short public life talking about what people earn, keep, owe, and fear losing.

We have quietly agreed not to notice.

Money is the one subject a congregation will forgive a pastor for nearly anything except raising. We will sit still for hard preaching on pride, on anger, on doubt. Bring up money and the room changes temperature. That reaction is worth paying attention to, because we do not guard what does not matter to us. We guard what we are afraid to lose. The flinch is information.

Here is the question the Bible actually asks, and it is not the one we expect. Its main concern about money is not how much you have. It is not even, first, what you do with it. It is what it is doing to you.

Because money, in the teaching of Jesus, is never only a tool. He says something about it he says about nothing else. He gives it a name and treats it as a rival. "You cannot serve God and money", and the word he used was *mammon*, an Aramaic word he personifies, a master with a throne and a claim. He never does this with sex. He never does this with power. Only money gets named as a rival god, because money, more than almost anything we handle, has the strange ability to stop being something we own and start being something that owns us.

I want to be careful, because the church has gone wrong here in two opposite directions. One made God a means to money: give, and he will make you rich. That is mammon in a clerical collar. The other made money itself the sin, so that a paid-off house or a good meal becomes a failure of holiness. That is a different lie. The Bible does neither. It does not flatter wealth, and it does not romanticize poverty. It tells the truth about a power, and it offers to set us free.

And it tells that truth to all of us, which is the part we resist. We assume the warnings are for the rich, by which we always mean someone richer than we are. The man with the boat aims the verse at the man with the yacht. Everyone has someone above them to point it at, so it never lands. But mammon does not check your balance before it goes to work on you. The pull is the same in a trailer and a penthouse.

Here is the line that holds everything together: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." Read it slowly, because the order is not what we assume. We think the heart leads and the money follows, that we fund what we already love. Jesus says it runs the other way. The treasure leads, and the heart follows it, the way a compass needle turns north whether or not you meant it to.

That is either very bad news or very good, depending on what you do with it. It means you cannot simply decide to care less about money by trying harder. But it also means there is a door. Move the treasure, and the heart will follow it out.

That is the hope underneath the whole thing, and it is not a technique for getting rich or a guilt trip for being comfortable. It is freedom. The closed fist, gripping, calculating, never quite able to rest because the number is never quite enough, can become an open hand. Not by willpower. Not by shame. By the slow, real work of moving our treasure to a place that cannot be lost, until the heart, that obedient compass, finally turns and follows it home.

You cannot serve both. That is not a threat. It is a mercy.

*[Where Your Treasure Is: What the Bible Says About Money, and the Heart It Means to Free](/where-your-treasure-is) is available now as an ebook.*

chapters.title: Why Christians Are Bad at Talking About Money
chapters.summary: The church talks about sex, doubt, and death more honestly than it talks about money. The silence is not accidental, it protects something, and what it protects deserves to be exposed.
chapters.body:
Here is a strange fact about the modern church. We have gotten reasonably good, over the last generation, at talking honestly about hard things. We talk about sexual brokenness, about depression and anxiety, about doubt, about marriage in crisis, about addiction, about grief. The culture of confession and vulnerability has entered the church, and mostly for the better. A person can stand up in many congregations today and admit to almost anything.

Except money. Money remains the last taboo. You will hear a man confess an affair before you hear him tell you his salary. You will hear a woman describe her battle with anxiety before she tells you how much debt she is carrying. We will discuss the most intimate failures of the flesh and the spirit, and then fall completely silent about the number in the bank account. Something is being protected by that silence, and it is worth asking what.

## The Manipulation Hangover

Part of the reason is that the church has genuinely poisoned this well. A generation of Christians grew up watching money-hungry ministries treat their faith as a revenue stream, the televangelist demanding seed faith offerings from people who could not afford them, the prosperity preacher flying private jets purchased with the widow's mite, the constant, grinding appeal for funds that made the whole enterprise feel like a business dressed up as worship. Anyone who lived through that has a reflexive suspicion of any preacher who brings up money, and honestly, they are right to.

So thoughtful pastors overcorrect. Determined not to be the money-grubbing charlatan, we avoid the subject almost entirely. We preach on money once a year, apologetically, hedged with disclaimers, and then retreat to safer ground. And in fleeing the manipulator, we have abandoned the field to him. The only people talking about money in the church are the ones exploiting it, precisely because the honest teachers have decided the topic is too dirty to touch. The abuse has silenced the very people who should be correcting it.

> We were so afraid of being the preacher who talks about money for the wrong reasons that we became the preacher who never talks about it at all. And Jesus talked about it constantly.

## Money as Confession

There is a deeper reason for the silence, and it goes to the heart of why money is so hard to discuss. Your finances are the most honest confession you will ever make. You can lie about almost anything else. You can present a curated version of your marriage, your faith, your character. But your bank statement does not lie. It records exactly what you value, what you fear, what you serve. It is a spiritual X-ray, and it shows the bones.

This is why money talk feels so threatening. To open your finances to another person is to let them see what you actually worship, not what you claim to worship. A man might genuinely believe he loves God and trusts him for the future, right up until his spending reveals a life organized entirely around self-protection and status. The gap between our stated values and our spending is often enormous, and money conversations expose that gap in a way nothing else does. We keep money private not because it is unimportant but because it is too revealing. It tells the truth about us, and we would rather not know it.

## The Idol That Hides Best

Jesus said no one can serve two masters, and he named the second master specifically: money. Not power, not sex, not pride, money, mammon, the accumulation of wealth. He treated money as a rival deity, a competing god with its own priesthood and its own promises, capable of commanding the whole allegiance of a human heart. And the thing about the idol of money is that it is the idol that hides best. The greedy person almost never knows they are greedy. Every rich person can point to someone richer and feel comparatively modest. The love of money disguises itself as prudence, as responsibility, as good stewardship, as simply being sensible.

This is why the silence is so dangerous. The idol thrives in the dark. As long as we never talk honestly about money, the god of mammon can rule half the hearts in the congregation without anyone noticing, because everyone is too polite to bring it up. We would confront a man about his drinking or his temper. We will not confront him about his greed, because greed is respectable, because greed is what our whole culture is built to produce, and because confronting it would require examining our own accounts first, which none of us wants to do.

## The Discipleship We Skip

Consider what this silence costs in terms of actual discipleship. If Jesus talked about money more than heaven and hell combined, and we talk about it once a year with apologies, then we have systematically failed to disciple people in one of the areas Jesus considered most important. We form Christians who have thought carefully about theology, prayer, evangelism, and sexual ethics, and who have never once been discipled in how to hold money, how to give, how to work, how to resist the god their entire economy is training them to serve.

The result is a church full of people who are theologically orthodox and financially indistinguishable from their unbelieving neighbors, same debt loads, same consumption patterns, same anxiety about money, same identity wrapped up in what they earn and own. We have discipled their doctrine and left their wallets in the hands of the culture. And then we wonder why the faith seems to make so little practical difference in how people actually live, when we have deliberately avoided the one topic Jesus used to expose the real condition of the heart.

## Learning to Speak

Recovering the ability to talk about money honestly does not mean returning to manipulation. It means the opposite. It means speaking about money the way Jesus did, frequently, directly, without embarrassment, and always in a way that exposes the idol rather than exploiting the anxiety. It means a pastor being willing to say hard things about greed without any personal financial benefit riding on the sermon. It means creating a church culture where a person can actually confess their financial struggles the way they confess their other struggles, and find help rather than judgment.

And it means self-implication, always. I cannot preach honestly about money if I am hiding my own relationship to it. The pastor who thunders about greed from a position of concealed comfort is a hypocrite, and the congregation can smell it. The only credible way to talk about money in the church is to talk about it as a fellow sinner still wrestling with the same idol, still finding the love of mammon rooted deeper in my own heart than I would like to admit, still learning to hold what I have with open hands. That kind of honesty is disarming precisely because it refuses the two positions people expect from a preacher on money, the manipulator who wants theirs and the coward who says nothing.

## The Class Discomfort

There is another layer to the silence, and it is one we are especially reluctant to admit: money talk exposes class differences that the church would rather pretend do not exist. When a congregation contains both the struggling family and the comfortable professional, honest money conversation becomes socially treacherous. The wealthy member does not want to seem to boast or to condescend; the struggling member does not want to seem to complain or to beg. So everyone agrees, without ever agreeing, to keep the actual numbers hidden, and the class divide is preserved by a mutual politeness that looks like kindness and functions like avoidance.

But this politeness comes at a cost. It means the struggling family suffers in silence, too ashamed to say they cannot afford the retreat, the youth trip, the giving campaign. It means the wealthy member never has their comfort challenged by real proximity to need. It means the church remains sorted by class beneath a surface of fellowship, everyone smiling and no one honest. The refusal to talk about money is partly a refusal to let the classes actually see each other, and in that refusal the church quietly accepts the world's arrangement rather than the kingdom's. Real community across the money divide requires the very honesty we have agreed to avoid.

## What Honest Money Talk Sounds Like

It is worth picturing what a healthier culture would actually sound like, because the alternative to manipulation is not silence but honesty, and honesty has a particular texture. It sounds like a pastor preaching on money as often and as directly as Jesus did, without apology and without personal benefit. It sounds like a small group where a person can say, I am in debt and I am afraid, and be met with help rather than judgment. It sounds like a mature believer being willing to say out loud that they have wrestled with greed, that they have felt the pull of mammon, that they do not have this fully figured out either.

It sounds, above all, like confession, the same confession we have learned to make about our other struggles, extended at last to the one we have kept hidden. When a Christian can say I have loved money more than God and I need help with this, the same way they might say I have struggled with lust or anger or doubt, the idol loses its power to hide. Confession drags it into the light, and in the light it withers. The church that recovers honest money talk is not a church that has become obsessed with money. It is a church that has finally brought the last dark corner of the heart into the healing light of the gospel.

## The Sermon That Costs the Preacher

There is a particular reason money is hard to preach that goes beyond manipulation and class, and it strikes closest to those of us in the pulpit. To preach honestly about money is to preach against ourselves, because we are as caught by mammon as anyone in the pews, and often more comfortably so. The pastor who denounces greed must first face the greed in his own heart, the anxiety about his own salary, the quiet ways he has organized his own life around security and status. It is far easier to preach on sins we do not struggle with than on the one we share with our congregation, and money is the sin we all share.

This is why the honest money sermon has a distinctive quality: it must be self-implicating, or it is a lie. The preacher who thunders about the love of money from a position of concealed comfort, who aims the warning at wealthier people down the road while quietly nursing his own attachment, has forfeited his credibility, and the congregation can sense it even when they cannot name it. The only sermon on money that lands is the one preached by a fellow struggler, standing inside the indictment rather than above it, confessing the pull of the idol in his own life even as he names it. I have preached money badly when I preached it safely, from a distance, as though it were someone else's problem. It is my problem. It is the problem of every one of us, and the sermon only works when the one preaching it admits he is the first sinner in the room.

## Recovering the Joy

It would be a mistake to leave the impression that recovering honest money talk is only about confronting sin, because the deepest reason to break the silence is joy. The Christians who have learned to talk openly about money, to give freely, to hold their possessions loosely, are not grim ascetics burdened by obligation. They are among the freest and most joyful people I know. They have escaped the anxiety that grips those who serve mammon, the endless comparison, the fear of loss, the exhausting vigilance of the accumulator. They give with gladness and receive with gratitude and hold everything with the open hands of people who have discovered they lack nothing that matters.

This joy is the great missing testimony in the church's silence about money. As long as we cannot speak of it, we cannot celebrate the freedom that comes from holding it rightly, and we leave people trapped in an anxiety the gospel means to heal. The point of breaking the taboo is not merely to expose the idol but to invite people into the liberty on the other side of it, the liberty of the person who has finally understood that they cannot serve God and money, and has chosen God, and has found, to their surprise, that in losing their grip on money they gained a joy no amount of it could ever buy. The last taboo needs to fall. Not so we can extract more from people, but so we can finally disciple them in the thing Jesus cared about most and we have avoided most, and lead them into the joy that waits on the far side of the silence. It is time to name it, starting with the one in our own accounts.

chapters.title: You Cannot Serve God and Money: What Jesus Meant by Mammon
chapters.summary: Jesus did not call money a tool. He gave it a name, mammon, and set it opposite God as a rival lord. "Money" is a thing you manage. Mammon is something that manages you.
chapters.body:
The verse most of us know, that no one can serve two masters, was not spoken to misers. Jesus said it on a hillside to ordinary people who carried the same mixture of ordinary ambition and ordinary worry that fills a congregation on any Sunday. The rival master he names is not an extreme case. It is the ordinary case.

He calls it mammon.

"No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24). Read it line by line. "No one can serve two masters." The Greek is *douleuō*, the slave word, not an employee who divides a shift between two jobs, but a slave, with a single lord whose claim is total. An employee can work for two employers. A slave cannot. The verse does not ask whether you find money demanding. It asks who holds the title to your life. The point is not that serving two masters is difficult. It is that it is structurally impossible. Someone holds the title, even if the slave does not know it yet.

"You cannot serve God and mammon." *Mammon* is Aramaic, and in Jesus' day it was the everyday, unremarkable word for your stuff, possessions, property, wealth. Jesus did not reach for a specialized term of rebuke. He reached for the ordinary word and turned it into a name. In verse 24, money is not a tool or a resource. It is a *kurios*, a lord, a master, set grammatically parallel to God, a rival for the same position. Jesus is not saying money can become a distraction. He is saying money occupies the same category as God. It makes a claim on the heart. It offers security, identity, status, a future. Those are not the functions of a tool. They are the functions of a lord.

The early church found the word striking enough to leave untranslated. Jerome kept *mammon* in the Latin Vulgate rather than converting it to *pecunia*. The King James kept it in 1611. Only in the twentieth century did versions begin rendering it simply "money", a choice that gains clarity and loses the personification in the same stroke. "Money" is a thing you manage. Mammon is something that manages you.

Tim Keller, in *Counterfeit Gods* (2009), called money "the most versatile" idol, because it can stand in for nearly every other, success, control, approval. And he says what the church has been slow to say: the idol of money is not primarily the problem of the very wealthy. It is the problem of anyone who trusts money to do what only God can do. The person anxious about financial security, who cannot imagine giving freely because the future feels too uncertain, is not miserly. They are afraid, and they are using money as the wall they have built against the fear. The wall is the idol. It does not have to be a very large wall.

Jacques Ellul, in *Money and Power* (1954), pressed further: money is a genuine spiritual power, and it has an agenda. It is not content to be held and used. It moves toward ownership. The person who thinks they are using money is being slowly transformed by it. None of this feels like worship. It feels like good sense. That is how a spiritual power works, not through dramatic temptation but through the gradual normalization of its logic, until its values are simply how we think.

Here is what the passage will not let us avoid. When we hear "you cannot serve God and mammon," we instinctively locate the target across the room, the extravagant spender, the aggressive accumulator, the one with more than us. But the verse gives us no exit. It addresses everyone who has two potential masters, and unless you are entirely without money, you have two. The rebuke belongs to us before it belongs to anyone else.

So what breaks the grip? Not less desire. Idols are not destroyed by removal, the heart immediately finds a replacement. They are displaced by a greater love. Jesus does not simply tell us to give money away. He tells us we cannot serve two masters, and then he shows us a better treasure. The open hand is not an absence of desire. It belongs to a person who has found something to hold that does not require the fist. The generous person is not someone who wants less. They are someone who has found more.
